title: How wrong is a line?
objectives: Measure the errors of a line on a table of points, and see why we square them.

screens.title: Fit by eye
screens.prose: Five points and the line $y = 2x + 1$. Each short stick runs from a point to the line. Move the line with the sliders until it looks as good as you can make it.
screens.question: For $y = 2x + 1$, how far is the line from the point at $x = 5$?

hints.text: Set the sliders back to $w$ = 2 and $b$ = 1 and read the fifth error.
The point is at 9, so the line is $11 - 9 = 2$ above it.

feedback.correct: The line gives 11 and the point is 9: a miss of 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out the line's value at $x = 5$, then compare with the point.

byKey.point: 9 is the point's height. The question is how far the line is from it.
byKey.line: 11 is where the line is at $x = 5$. Take away the point's 9.

explain.text: At $x = 5$ the line predicts 11 and the point is 9, so it misses by 2. You can see each miss, but saying how good a whole line is needs one number.

screens.title: Five errors
screens.prose: Machine learning writes $y = mx + c$ from functions l7 as $y = wx + b$: the same line, with the names machine learning uses. The **error** at a point is the prediction minus the actual value.
screens.question: Fill in the error of $y = 2x + 1$ at each point.

hints.text: Prediction minus actual: the third column minus the second.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the actual $y$ away from the prediction in each row.

explain.text: Each error is the prediction minus the actual value: $3 - 3 = 0$, $5 - 4 = 1$, $7 - 6 = 1$, $9 - 7 = 2$ and $11 - 9 = 2$. All are 0 or positive, so the line runs above the points.

screens.title: Add them up?
screens.prose: One idea for a single number: add the errors. For $y = 2x + 1$ they add to 6. Now try the flat line $y = 5.8$, which is the mean of the five $y$ values.
screens.question: What do the five errors of the flat line add up to?

hints.text: The errors are $5.8 - y$ for each point.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep the signs: misses below count as negative.

byKey.sizes: You added the sizes and dropped the signs. With signs, the misses above and below cancel to 0.
byKey.first: 2.8 is the first error only. Add all five, keeping their signs.

explain.text: The errors are 2.8, 1.8, −0.2, −1.2 and −3.2. They add to 0, a perfect score, although the line misses every point.

screens.title: A perfect zero?
screens.prose: A colleague says: “The flat line's errors add to 0, so it is a perfect fit. Better than $y = 2x + 1$, whose errors add to 6.”
screens.question: What is wrong with that?

options.text: Misses above cancel misses below, so 0 hides five misses
Nothing: a total of 0 means no error
options.why: Every point is missed; the total is 0 only because the signs cancel.

options.text: The flat line is the mean, so it must be best
options.why: The mean always makes the errors add to 0. It does not follow the slope at all.

options.text: 6 is closer to 0 than any other total
options.why: A total near 0 can hide big misses either side. It does not measure distance.

hints.text: Is the flat line close to any point?
Look at the signs in the Error column.
Positive and negative errors cancel when they are added.

feedback.correct: Adding raw errors lets misses cancel.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at the signs of the errors.

byKey.right: You trusted the 0. The flat line misses the first point by 2.8 and the last by 3.2; the signs cancel.

explain.text: Adding raw errors lets a miss above cancel a miss below. The flat line misses every point and still scores 0. We need a way to make every miss count.

screens.title: Square them
screens.prose: Square each error. A square is never negative, so nothing cancels. The result is the **squared error**.
screens.question: Fill in the squared errors of $y = 2x + 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply each error by itself.

explain.text: Squaring gives 0, 1, 1, 4 and 4. The two misses of 2 now count four times as much as a miss of 1. Every miss counts, and big misses count most.

screens.title: The flat line, squared
screens.prose: Here are the flat line's errors again.
screens.question: What do the flat line's five squared errors add up to?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each error, then add.

byKey.raw: That is the raw total. Square each error before adding.
byKey.no-square: You added the sizes, 9.2. Square each one first.

explain.text: The squares are 7.84, 3.24, 0.04, 1.44 and 10.24, which add to 22.8. The line $y = 2x + 1$ scores $0 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 4 = 10$. Squared, the flat line is clearly worse.

screens.title: Through every point
screens.prose: Three points: (1, 3), (2, 5) and (4, 9). The line is $y = 2x + 1$.
screens.question: What do its squared errors add up to on these three points?

hints.text: Check the line at each point.

feedback.correct: Every error is 0, so the sum is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out the line at each $x$.

byKey.count: 3 is the number of points. Each error is 0, so the sum is 0.

explain.text: The line passes through all three points, so every error is 0 and so is every square. A sum of 0 now really means no miss, because squares cannot cancel.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: For each point, $$\text{error} = \text{prediction} - \text{actual}, \qquad \text{squared error} = \text{error} \times \text{error}.$$ Squaring makes every miss count, and a big miss counts most: twice the miss is four times the squared error.
screens.question: A prediction is 10 and the actual value is 14. What is the squared error?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the error, then multiply it by itself.

byKey.neg: A negative times a negative is positive: $(-4)^2 = 16$.
byKey.size: 4 is the size of the miss. Square it: 16.

explain.text: The error is $10 - 14 = -4$. Its square is $(-4) \times (-4) = 16$, positive like every square.

screens.title: Two forecasters
screens.prose: Two forecasters predict the daily high temperature for a week of five working days. Their errors are below.
screens.question: Which forecaster has the smaller sum of squared errors?

options.text: B: its raw errors add to only 4
options.why: Raw sums let the four perfect days hide the miss of 4. Squared, B scores 16.
A's squares add to 5 and B's to 16.

byKey.b: You compared raw sums. One miss of 4 °C on Friday outweighs five misses of 1 °C once squared.

explain.text: A's squared errors add to 5 and B's to 16. One big miss can cost an energy trader more than many small ones, and squaring says so.

ideas: The error at a point is the prediction minus the actual value.
Adding raw errors lets misses above cancel misses below: the flat line $y = 5.8$ scores 0 and misses every point.
Squaring makes every miss count, and a big miss counts most: twice the miss is four times the square.

formula.name: Squared error
formula.note: Never negative, so misses cannot cancel.

summary.trap: A total error of 0 can hide large misses either side of the line.

quiz.prose: A line predicts 7 at a point whose actual value is 9.
quiz.question: What is the error, prediction minus actual?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the actual value from the prediction.

byKey.flipped: You did actual minus prediction. The error here is prediction minus actual, $7 - 9$.

explain.text: Prediction minus actual is $7 - 9 = -2$: the line is 2 below the point.

quiz.prose: A line's errors on four points are 1, −2, 0 and 3.
quiz.question: What do the squared errors add up to?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each error, then add.

byKey.raw: 2 is the raw total; the −2 cancelled part of the rest.
byKey.sizes: 6 adds the sizes. Square each first.
byKey.total-sq: You squared the raw total, 2. Square each error, then add.

explain.text: The squares are 1, 4, 0 and 9, which add to 14.

quiz.prose: Line P's errors are 3, −3, 3, −3. Line Q's are 1, 1, 1, 1.
quiz.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: Q is closer: its squared errors add to 4, P's to 36
P is closer, because its errors add to 0
options.why: P's errors cancel. Each miss is 3; squared they add to 36.

options.text: They are equally close to the points
options.why: Q misses by 1 each time and P by 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square before you add.

explain.text: P's errors add to 0 only because they cancel. Squared, P scores 36 and Q scores 4. Q is closer.
